EXPANSION OF COMMERCIAL ZONES AND THE PUBLIC INTEREST
In the prior sections of this report we have confined our discussion to the economic evidence and statutory guidelines relevant to the proper present-day interpretation and application of the exemptions provided by sections 202(c) and 203(b)(8) of the Act. We have concluded that the original population-mileage formula no longer describes the size and structure of contemporary cities. We must now focus on considerations of a different nature, for any action we take in this matter must be coupled with a finding that the adopted rules are compatible with the public interest and promote the goals of the National Transportation 64 Policy. This policy is stated in the preamble to the Act as follows:
It is hereby declared to be the national transportation policy of the Congress to provide for fair and impartial regulation of all modes of transportation subject to the provisions of this Act, so administered as to recognize and preserve the inherent advantages of each; to promote safe, adequate, economical, and efficient service and foster sound economic conditions in transportation and among the several carriers; to encourage the establishment and maintenance of reasonable charges for transportation services, without unjust discriminations, undue preferences or advantages, or unfair or destructive competitive practices; to cooperate with the several States and the duly authorized officials thereof; and to encourage fair wages and equitable working conditions; - all to the end of developing, coordinating, and preserving a national transportation system by water, highway, and rail, as well as other means, adequate to meet the needs of the commerce of the United States, of the Postal Service, and of the national defense. All of the provisions of this Act shall be administered and enforced with a view to carrying out the above declaration of policy. 54 Stat. 899 (1940).
